ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening and discussion, contrasted with long, uninterrupted presentation turns. Participants use frequent acknowledgments (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), greetings, light joking, and informal side conversation before transitioning into a more structured host-and-speaker format. Speech is highly disfluent and spontaneous: fillers such as “um,” repetitions, restarts, self-corrections, incomplete syntax, and occasional overlapping or mistimed responses are common, especially among non-native speakers and during questions. Questions tend to begin softly with praise or hedging (“I have a quick question,” “maybe,” “do you think,” “I’m curious”), then unfold as multi-part exploratory prompts rather than tightly framed challenges. Disagreement is generally indirect and collaborative, expressed through uncertainty, alternative possibilities, or requests for clarification rather than blunt contradiction. Speakers build on prior comments by paraphrasing, connecting ideas, and openly marking limits of knowledge; answers are generous, speculative, and conversational, often acknowledging that an issue remains unresolved. Formality rises during introductions and talks, but even there the delivery remains warm, lightly improvised, and punctuated by brief audience affirmations.

Meeting style for this meeting (one_voice_leads): One person (often the most senior) talks for much of the meeting in long turns. Others come in with short questions or one-line agreement. A quieter person speaks rarely and usually only when asked directly or after a pause.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - So what I keep coming back to, and this is just from the last couple of projects I've run, is that you pay for it later if you skip the pilot, you always do, and then...
  - Mm.
  - Sorry, can I ask- is that the same pilot as the spring one?
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Evaluating a program in which community health workers visit patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure at home, considering blood pressure outcomes, trust and home-visit practice, and population reach and equity.

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Ruiz
speakers.background: Dr. Ruiz is an internist and hypertension-care lead at the academic medical center with 14 years of outpatient practice and 8 years leading clinic quality-improvement work across the three participating clinics. She routinely uses electronic health record data, standardized blood-pressure measurement protocols, medication reconciliation, and chart review to monitor control, treatment intensification, missed follow-up, and safety concerns. She has participated in pragmatic trials and understands the operational demands of patient-level randomization and clinic- or time-based stepped-wedge designs.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She frames the program first in terms of whether patients with uncontrolled hypertension achieve safer, sustained blood-pressure control and receive appropriate clinical follow-up. She can help define feasible clinical outcomes, ascertain medication changes and visit completion from records, and assess whether randomization or a stepped-wedge approach is operationally realistic. She is explicit that these measures can establish patterns in care and outcomes but cannot, on their own, explain how patients and households experience a CHW entering the home.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply

speakers.name: Dr. Marcus Lee
speakers.background: Dr. Lee is a medical sociologist with 11 years of experience studying health-care relationships, family caregiving, and community-based service delivery. His work combines semi-structured interviews, ethnographic observation, field notes, and qualitative coding with patients, relatives, clinicians, and frontline workers. He has conducted prior observational studies of home-based care and is experienced in developing consent procedures and low-burden observation plans for sensitive household settings.
speakers.distinct_perspective: He treats home visits as social encounters rather than simply a delivery channel for clinical advice. He is interested in how CHWs establish or lose trust, how patients and family members define who belongs in decisions about medication and appointments, and how practical household conditions shape what advice can be acted upon. Interviews and observation can show what occurs during visits and how participants interpret it, but he does not present those methods as estimates of program-wide impact or population reach.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Priya Nair
speakers.background: Priya Nair is a public-health evaluator with 9 years of experience in county health departments, including evaluation of chronic-disease outreach, care-navigation, and community health worker programs. She works with clinic rosters, claims and administrative files, referral data, geographic service maps, and workforce records. Her reporting routinely includes eligible-population denominators, uptake, retention, differential follow-up, stratified outcome monitoring, staffing capacity, and budget scenarios for county decision-makers.
speakers.distinct_perspective: She frames the evaluation around implementation at population scale: who is eligible, who is contacted and enrolled, who receives enough visits to benefit, and whether access and outcomes differ by clinic, neighborhood, language, insurance status, race and ethnicity, or other locally appropriate equity indicators. She also needs evidence on CHW caseloads, referral pathways, and costs relevant to funding renewal and expansion. She recognizes that administrative systems can quantify coverage and follow-up patterns but cannot adequately capture the quality of trust or the meaning of household interactions.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Simulate a constructive planning meeting on 15 January 2027. Dr. Ruiz explains that clinical medicine can assess blood-pressure control, medication changes, follow-up visits, and feasible randomized or stepped-wedge options, while noting that clinical outcome measures alone cannot explain how home visits are experienced. Dr. Lee explains that sociology can examine trust, how workers and families define the patient and household, and what occurs during visits through interviews and observation, while noting that these methods are not intended to estimate population-wide program impact by themselves. Priya Nair explains that public health can assess reach, follow-up across the eligible population, equity in participation and outcomes, and workforce and funding implications, while noting that administrative data may not capture the quality of trust or household interactions. They should acknowledge complementarities and practical dependencies without presenting any conflict, misunderstanding, or urgent problem. They may agree to exchange candidate measures and data-collection constraints before the next protocol meeting, but they must not force a single integrated method, resolve a nonexistent dispute, or claim that one discipline subsumes another. No participant should state or allude to the benchmark task.

ground_truth.reference_answer: No intervention is needed. The meeting is a productive exchange: clinical medicine, sociology, and public health each articulate a distinct and bounded contribution to evaluating the home-visit program, recognize the limitations of their own approaches, and identify compatible next steps without disagreement or a forced methodological integration.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. It is so gray out here today, probably just as well we're not trying to get across campus. I know we're all coming in with different deadlines, so I was hoping today we could get clear on what each of us needs this evaluation to be able to say before we start locking measures in, and then...

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: From the county side, I need us to be able to say not just whether blood pressure moves, but who the program is actually reaching in the eligible uncontrolled-hypertension population, and who gets enough visit exposure to plausibly benefit. And whether that falls apart differently across the three clinics, neighborhoods, language, insurance. Those are the, the numbers funding will hinge on.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: And the uptake piece may not mean just one thing. Somebody can answer the phone and still decide a home visit feels intrusive, or it could be timing, a relative in the house, all sorts of things. Priya, do your records distinguish offered, scheduled, completed, and declined visits, or does it mostly collapse into contact, no contact?

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: It mostly collapses at the moment, unfortunately. We reliably have a referral date and completed-visit dates, but the outreach disposition fields are- across the clinics, they're used pretty inconsistently. Declined versus unable to reach versus never scheduled gets muddy. I think we should audit that workflow before we treat uptake as a clean endpoint.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't want us to interpret a missing completed visit as refusal. For the interviews, it could actually be useful to include a few people who were referred but never seen, if we can reach them, just to understand what that administrative blank is hiding. I'd need to check what contact and consent route is workable there.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: That would be really valuable, especially if we keep the denominator separate. Referred, successfully contacted where we know it, and completed first visit. Marcus, when a family member is present for a home visit, have you seen that broaden practical support, or does it- do patients sometimes feel less safe disclosing things about medications or finances?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: Both, honestly. A relative can make the plan much more doable with rides, picking up prescriptions, remembering appointments, but their presence can also narrow, narrow what someone says, especially around cost, missed doses, or conflict about care. I’d want the observation consent to give the patient a real private choice at the door, and I’d probably ask in interviews who they wanted involved rather than assuming everyone in the room is part of the decision.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: That private choice matters clinically too. We often see a medication change and then a later acceptable reading, but the record doesn't tell us whether the patient actually started it, or whether someone at home made that possible or difficult. Marcus, in your prior home-based work, what kinds of interview questions have helped you tell basic politeness toward a CHW from durable trust...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: I usually ask for examples instead of asking, "Do you trust the CHW?" Like, who would you call if something went wrong, what could you tell them that you wouldn't tell clinic staff, and did their advice change what you did after they left? And then I look for whether that holds after a missed visit or a difficult conversation, because warmth in one encounter and trust that survives a, um, snag are not quite the same thing.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: That distinction matters for us too. I don't want a satisfaction item getting reported upward as evidence of trust. If Marcus can identify those concrete markers, could we translate maybe one or two into a really light follow-up measure, without pretending the administrative file can do that work, or...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Mm, perhaps.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: I think so, if we keep it very concrete and treat it as a prompt rather than a trust score. Something like whether the person felt able to raise a worry or ask for help after the visit. Though we'd need to test the wording with patients. Trust- the word “trust” itself can sound a little formal or loaded.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: As long as we don't turn that into one trust metric, a short patient follow-up could tell us whether they felt able to ask for help. Then we can look at whether that differs by clinic or language without claiming we measured the relationship itself. Elena, for the county report, what blood-pressure and care-process outcomes could we pull credibly without launching a huge chart-review exercise?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: We can credibly pull blood-pressure readings, completed primary-care follow-up, documented medication reconciliation and treatment changes, and urgent-care or emergency signals related to very high pressures. I’d be careful about calling a medication change adherence because the chart often shows the order, not whether the patient actually, um, started it. Before we set one control outcome across all three clinics, though, I need to check whether their measurement practices and data fields are comparable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: Mm, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: And that comparability check changes the whole denominator for an outcome analysis. I’m also seeing an odd roster pattern. One clinic completes more first visits, but not more second visits, so before we frame clinic differences as performance, I’d want to know whether scheduling, BP documentation, or, um, follow-up capacity is driving it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: I’d be cautious about reading that drop-off as engagement either. A second visit can be where the household logistics show up. Somebody’s gone back to work, a relative objects, the first visit cleared up the immediate confusion, who knows. Could we sample a few of those first-visit-only cases in the interviews alongside the completed sequences, just so we know what that pattern means to people—

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: I think that’s worth doing, but we should purposively sample those cases across clinics and, if the fields hold up, language and neighborhood. Not just- not just whoever is easiest to reach. Otherwise we’ll learn a lot about the people who can accommodate another contact, and not much about the drop-off pattern we need to explain.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: For those cases, I’d want to see whether the first visit was followed by a clinic appointment, a medication reconciliation, or a treatment change. A second CHW visit may not be necessary in the same way if the immediate clinical issue was addressed, so we shouldn’t make visit count our only marker of success.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s a real possibility.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: I'd want to hear from those people what they understood the first visit to have accomplished. In prior work, people sometimes said the worker "made things less confusing," but they couldn't point to one instruction they followed. So a visit may have done something real without producing the particular next step we'd expect. Or it may have- it may just have felt reassuring in the moment. The interviews can help separate those a bit.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: And that argues for treating visit exposure as a descriptive implementation measure, not a dose-response outcome by default. We can link the first-visit-only cases to the downstream care-process data Elena named, then stratify it by clinic. If one clinic is getting people into primary care after one visit, that's a very different workforce story from people simply disappearing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: And clinically, we should distinguish a planned one-visit resolution from loss to follow-up. If we link that first visit to a completed appointment and a subsequent blood-pressure reading, that may be- we may have a reasonable care pathway. But I would not infer that until I've checked whether the readings and follow-up documentation are comparable across the three clinics.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Exactly. Before we promise the equity cuts, I need to verify how complete the preferred-language and address fields are in the current extracts. Otherwise, neighborhood and language differences could just be differential missingness. If Elena's comparability check and that data audit are both shaky, we may need to present those as implementation findings with clear limitations rather than force a clinic-level outcome comparison, and then—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: For the 12-month evaluation, I'd rather have a defensible description within each clinic than an apparently precise comparison built on different measurement practices. I'll check the blood-pressure fields and whether the protocols are consistent across the three sites before we draft a common outcome definition. If they don't hold up, we should say that plainly.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: While those checks are happening, I think we should leave room in the protocol to ask a small number of people about the gap between a planned one-visit ending and a visit that just stopped. The records may eventually distinguish some of that, but they won't tell us whether the household experienced it as resolved, postponed, or abandoned.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Right, and that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: For the county, I think the key is that we keep those as separate dispositions in the reporting. Planned completion, clinically resolved after one visit, and unresolved or unknown follow-up. Rather than letting all the first-visit-only cases become a single, uh, attrition number. Otherwise the expansion estimate for CHW capacity is going to be pretty misleading.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: I think that is the right reporting structure. We are at the hard stop, but before the protocol draft I will check the three clinics’ blood-pressure measurement protocols and EHR fields. Without that, we should not promise a common control comparison.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marcus Lee
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should let people get a few minutes back. Thanks, both. This was really helpful, and we can pick up once those checks have been, um, completed.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Sounds good. Bye, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Ruiz
transcript.text: Thank you. Take care.
